name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Three critical research areas of modern biotechnology

questiontext.text: Which of the following is explicitly listed in NCERT as one of the three critical research areas of biotechnology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Critical Research Areas
Biotechnology focuses on three critical research areas: providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme, creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act, and downstream processing technologies to purify the target protein or organic compound.

Step 2: Evaluation of Other Processes
Synthesising synthetic organochlorines, replacing tissue culture with cattle breeding, or eliminating downstream processing are contrary to biotechnological goals. Providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism or pure enzyme represents the first primary research pillar.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The fundamental research area identified is providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme.

answer.text: Eliminating downstream processing stages to lower production costs
Synthesising broad spectrum synthetic organochlorine pesticides
Providing the best catalyst in the form of improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme
Replacing cellular tissue culture with conventional cattle breeding

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Primary objective of downstream processing technologies

questiontext.text: In industrial bioprocess biotechnology, downstream processing technologies are primarily employed for which purpose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of Downstream Processing
Downstream processing refers to the stages of bioprocessing that occur after the biosynthetic phase in bioreactors. Its objective is the recovery, separation, and purification of the desired biosynthetic product to commercial standards.

Step 2: Distinction from Upstream Stages
Upstream processing involves strain improvement, media formulation, and culturing conditions. Downstream processing deals specifically with purifying and formulating the synthesized protein or organic compound.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Downstream processing technologies are employed for the purification and isolation of the desired protein or organic compound.

answer.text: Direct insertion of recombinant plasmids into competent bacterial hosts
Formulation of initial nutrient agar media for microbial incubation
Purification and isolation of the desired protein or organic compound
Induction of somatic embryogenesis in excised plant explants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Impact of Green Revolution on global food supply

questiontext.text: The Green Revolution succeeded in increasing the global food supply primarily by which degree and through which factors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Assessment of Green Revolution
The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply. This substantial increase was achieved partly through improved crop varieties, but primarily through better management practices and intensive application of agrochemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides.

Step 2: Evaluation of Agricultural Metrics
The food supply was tripled rather than doubled or quadrupled, and the Green Revolution did not utilize transgenic crops or eliminate chemical inputs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Green Revolution tripled the food supply through improved crop varieties, better management practices, and agrochemicals.

answer.text: Doubling food production exclusively through the use of transgenic insect-resistant crops
Eliminating reliance on chemical fertilisers and irrigation systems globally
Quadrupling agricultural yields relying solely on organic biofertilisers
Tripling food supply through improved crop varieties, better management practices, and agrochemicals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Limitations of agrochemicals for developing world farmers

questiontext.text: Why is agrochemical-based agriculture considered inadequate as a sole long-term strategy for farmers in the developing world?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Economic and Agronomic Constraints
For farmers in the developing world, synthetic agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides) are often too expensive to sustain. Furthermore, yield increases with existing high-yielding varieties have reached an agronomic plateau where conventional breeding techniques cannot achieve further substantial gains.

Step 2: Biological Reality
Agrochemicals do not halt crop cellular respiration, nor do conventional crops produce sterile seeds. Pests also develop resistance to agrochemicals over repeated applications.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Agrochemical-based farming is limited because agrochemicals are too expensive and conventional breeding cannot yield further significant gains with existing varieties.

answer.text: Agrochemicals eliminate all soil microorganisms responsible for carbon dioxide assimilation
Agrochemicals are often too expensive and conventional breeding cannot achieve further yield increases with existing varieties
Conventional plant breeding produces exclusively sterile plants that fail to produce seeds
Agrochemicals permanently halt cellular respiration in all cultivated crop varieties

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Definition of cellular totipotency in plant biology

questiontext.text: The biological capacity of an explant or a single plant cell to regenerate into a whole plant under in vitro culture conditions is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Totipotency
Totipotency is the inherent capacity of a plant cell or explant (any excised plant part) to divide, differentiate, and regenerate into a whole functional plant when provided with appropriate nutrients and hormonal stimuli under sterile conditions.

Step 2: Distinction from Related Concepts
Micropropagation is the commercial technique of generating thousands of plants, while totipotency is the physiological property of the plant cells that makes micropropagation possible.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cellular capacity to generate a whole plant from an explant is totipotency.

answer.text: Somaclonal variation
Totipotency
Micropropagation
Pluripotency

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Nutritional and hormonal constituents of culture medium

questiontext.text: Which combination of substances represents the essential constituents of a nutrient medium required for supporting in vitro plant tissue culture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Tissue Culture Medium Requirements
To sustain cell division, morphogenesis, and growth in vitro, the culture medium must provide an energy/carbon source (commonly sucrose), inorganic salts (macronutrients and micronutrients), vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins.

Step 2: Assessment of Incompatible Components
Substances like ethanol, heavy metals, or animal serum are not standard components of plant culture media, and an available carbon source like sucrose is mandatory.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The essential constituents comprise a carbon source like sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins.

answer.text: Starch granules, animal serum, antibiotic mixtures, and pure ethanol
Pure glycerol, heavy metals, cellulose fibres, and gaseous ethylene exclusively
Deionized water, concentrated mineral acids, and gibberellic acid only
A carbon source such as sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Micropropagation and genetic characteristics of somaclones

questiontext.text: Plants regenerated on a commercial scale through micropropagation are described as somaclones because they:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of Somaclones
Micropropagation produces thousands of plantlets through mitotic cell divisions from an initial explant. Because no sexual recombination occurs, all regenerated plants are genetically identical to each other and to the parent plant from which they originated, making them somaclones.

Step 2: Evaluation of Plausibility
Somaclones do not undergo polyploidization, nor do they carry foreign insecticidal genes unless genetically transformed, and they retain normal cell walls.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plants produced through micropropagation are somaclones because they are genetically identical to each other and to the original parent plant.

answer.text: Express foreign insecticidal crystal proteins in their chloroplasts
Lack cell walls and are bounded solely by plasma membranes
Are genetically identical to each other as well as to the original parent plant
Possess doubled chromosome sets compared to parental diploid tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Physiological basis of obtaining virus free plants

questiontext.text: Why does apical or axillary meristem culture successfully produce virus-free plants even when the donor mother plant is systemically infected with a virus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Virus Exclusion in Meristems
Plant viruses move systemically throughout the plant body primarily via vascular channels (phloem). The rapidly dividing apical and axillary meristems lack functional vascular bundles. Furthermore, the rate of mitotic cell division in the promeristem exceeds the rate of viral translocation and replication.

Step 2: Analysis of Plausibility
Meristematic cells are thin-walled, unlignified, do not produce chemical antibiotics, and divide mitotically rather than through meiosis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Meristem culture yields virus-free plants because vascular tissues are absent in the meristem and rapid cell division outpaces viral replication.

answer.text: Spontaneous meiotic recombination in meristem cells deletes all foreign viral genomes
The shoot tip possesses a thick, lignified suberin barrier that completely excludes viruses
The meristematic zone lacks functional vascular tissues and its high rate of cell division outpaces viral replication
Meristematic cells synthesize broad-spectrum chemical antibiotics that hydrolyse viral capsids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Isolation of naked plant protoplasts for somatic hybridisation

questiontext.text: Naked protoplasts utilized in somatic hybridisation are isolated from single plant cells by digesting which cellular structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Isolation of Protoplasts
A protoplast is a plant cell whose outer rigid cellulosic cell wall has been enzymatically removed using cellulase and pectinase. The resulting naked protoplast is bounded solely by its living plasma membrane.

Step 2: Integrity of Membrane Systems
The plasma membrane, nuclear envelope, and vacuolar tonoplast must remain completely intact to preserve cellular viability during somatic fusion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Naked protoplasts are isolated by enzymatically digesting the plant cell wall.

answer.text: Tonoplast
Cell wall
Nuclear envelope
Plasma membrane

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Significance and limitations of somatic hybridisation in pomato

questiontext.text: The development of pomato demonstrated the feasibility of somatic hybridisation. Which statement accurately highlights both its biological achievement and its commercial limitation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biological Feasibility of Pomato
Pomato was created by isolating and fusing naked protoplasts of tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum*) and potato (*Solanum tuberosum*). This proved that somatic hybridisation can unite genomes from two different plant varieties without sexual crossing.

Step 2: Agronomic Limitation
However, the regenerated hybrid plant did not possess all the desired combinations of commercial traits from both parents, rendering it unsuitable for viable commercial utilization.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pomato successfully combined tomato and potato genomes via somatic fusion, but lacked the desired combination of characteristics for commercial utilization.

answer.text: It produced an insect-resistant plant by expressing Bt toxin, but was restricted by international patent laws
It yielded high commercial profits by producing edible tubers and fruits, but failed to grow under field irrigation
It combined tomato and potato genomes by somatic protoplast fusion, but the hybrid lacked the desired combination of characteristics for commercial utilization
It overcame sexual incompatibility, but failed to undergo mitosis because protoplasts cannot regenerate cell walls

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q11 - Definition of Genetically Modified Organisms in agriculture

questiontext.text: Plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered through intentional genetic manipulation are officially designated as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of GMO
Any living organism—whether plant, bacterium, fungus, or animal—whose genome has been deliberately altered using genetic manipulation (recombinant DNA technology) is defined as a Genetically Modified Organism (GMO).

Step 2: Comparison with Other Classes
Somaclonal variants arise during in vitro propagation without foreign gene insertion, and somatic hybrids result from protoplast fusion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Organisms with artificially altered genes are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs).

answer.text: Somaclonal Variants
Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs)
Somatic Hybrids
Spontaneous Mutants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q12 - Nutritional enrichment of Golden Rice with Vitamin A

questiontext.text: Golden rice is a genetically engineered crop variety developed primarily to address which nutritional deficiency in human diets?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nutritional Objective of Golden Rice
Golden rice is a transgenic variety of rice (*Oryza sativa*) engineered to biosynthesise beta-carotene, a biochemical precursor of Vitamin A, in its edible endosperm.

Step 2: Target Health Condition
This biofortified crop was created specifically to combat dietary Vitamin A deficiency and prevent associated eye diseases, including night blindness and xerophthalmia, in populations heavily reliant on rice as a staple.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Golden rice has been genetically modified to be enriched in Vitamin A.

answer.text: Essential amino acid deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency
Vitamin A deficiency
Iron and calcium deficiency

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q13 - Agronomic benefits of genetically modified crops

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs two distinct agricultural advantages conferred on crop plants through genetic modification as described in NCERT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Documented Benefits of GM Crops
According to NCERT, genetic modification has: made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); reduced reliance on chemical pesticides; reduced post-harvest losses; increased efficiency of mineral usage to prevent premature exhaustion of soil fertility; and enhanced nutritional value of food.

Step 2: Critique of Distractors
Transgenic plants do not cease transpiration, eliminate nitrate uptake, synthesize organophosphates, or switch permanently to anaerobic fermentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The valid pair of advantages is enhanced abiotic stress tolerance and increased efficiency of mineral usage preventing early soil exhaustion.

answer.text: Enhanced tolerance to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat) and increased efficiency of mineral usage to prevent early exhaustion of soil fertility
Synthesis of broad-spectrum organophosphate chemicals and replacement of xylem with phloem
Conversion of aerobic respiration into permanent anaerobic fermentation in full sunlight
Complete cessation of cellular transpiration and elimination of nitrate assimilation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q14 - Bacterial source of insecticidal Bt toxin protein

questiontext.text: The insecticidal crystal protein (Bt toxin) incorporated into bio-pesticidal crops is naturally produced by which bacterium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Source of Bt Toxin
Bt toxin is an insecticidal protein produced naturally during sporulation by the soil bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis*.

Step 2: Assessment of Other Bacteria
*Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is used as a plant vector, *E. coli* is a cloning host, and *Thermus aquaticus* provides Taq polymerase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Bt toxin is naturally synthesized by *Bacillus thuringiensis*.

answer.text: Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Escherichia coli
Thermus aquaticus
Bacillus thuringiensis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q15 - Activation of Bt protoxin by alkaline gut pH

questiontext.text: Why does the insecticidal protein crystal of Bacillus thuringiensis not kill the producing bacterium itself?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Inactive State of Bt Toxin
Inside *Bacillus thuringiensis*, the toxin is accumulated as an inactive crystalline protein known as a protoxin.

Step 2: Activation Conditions
Because it is in an inactive crystalline form, it is non-toxic to the bacterium. Only upon ingestion by a susceptible insect does the alkaline pH of the insect midgut solubilise the protein crystals, allowing proteases to cleave it into the active toxin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The toxin does not harm the bacterium because it exists as an inactive protoxin requiring the alkaline pH of the insect gut for activation.

answer.text: The bacterium secretes a continuous supply of anti-toxin antibodies
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin and requires the alkaline pH of the insect gut to solubilise and activate it
The toxin only binds to eukaryotic ribosomes and spares prokaryotic 70S ribosomes
The bacterium encloses the toxin within an impermeable thick cuticular wall

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q16 - Cytotoxic action of activated Bt toxin on midgut

questiontext.text: Once activated in the insect alimentary canal, how does the Bt toxin cause the death of the targeted pest?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Lytic Pore Formation
The solubilised and activated Bt toxin binds specifically to receptors on the apical microvillar membrane of midgut epithelial cells in susceptible insects.

Step 2: Consequences of Pore Insertion
This binding leads to oligomerization and insertion into the membrane, forming lytic pores. These pores trigger osmotic swelling, cell lysis, destruction of the gut lining, and ultimately death of the insect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The activated Bt toxin binds to midgut epithelial cells, creating pores that cause cell swelling, lysis, and death.

answer.text: It blocks mitochondrial ATP synthase in Malpighian tubules, halting excretion
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing continuous synaptic tetany in the ventral nerve cord
It binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells, creating pores that cause cell swelling, lysis, and death
It prevents cuticular chitin deposition, causing lethal desiccation during moulting

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q17 - Specific cry genes controlling cotton bollworms in crops

questiontext.text: Which specific Bt toxin genes were isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis and incorporated into cotton to control cotton bollworms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gene Specificity for Cotton Bollworms
Different cry genes encode insecticidal proteins with targeted specificity against distinct insect pests. In Bt cotton, resistance against cotton bollworms is conferred by the introduction of the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb.

Step 2: Contrast with Corn Borer
The cryIAb gene specifically controls the corn borer, not cotton bollworms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cotton bollworms are controlled by the proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb.

answer.text: cryIAb and cryIIAb
cryIAb and cryIIAc
cryIAa and cryIAb
cryIAc and cryIIAb

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q18 - Pest specificity of different cry toxin genes

questiontext.text: A farmer intends to protect a maize field from corn borer and a cotton field from cotton bollworm. Which combination of Bt toxin genes must be expressed in the respective transgenic crops?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Specificity of Cry Proteins
Bt toxins exhibit strict insect-group specificity. According to NCERT: (1) the protein encoded by the gene cryIAb controls corn borer in crops such as maize; (2) the proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms in cotton crops.

Step 2: Analysis of Requirements
Thus, maize requires cryIAb for corn borer protection, whereas cotton requires cryIAc and cryIIAb for bollworm resistance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The farmer must use cryIAb in maize against corn borer, and cryIAc along with cryIIAb in cotton against cotton bollworm.

answer.text: cryIAb in maize against corn borer, and cryIAc and cryIIAb in cotton against cotton bollworm
cryIIAb in maize against corn borer, and cryIAb in cotton against cotton bollworm
cryIAc in maize against corn borer, and cryIAb in cotton against cotton bollworm
cryIAb in both maize and cotton crops against all lepidopteran pests

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q19 - Parasitic nematode infecting roots of tobacco plants

questiontext.text: Which parasitic nematode infects the root system of tobacco plants, leading to a substantial reduction in agricultural yield?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Tobacco Pest
*Meloidogyne incognita* is a widespread root-knot nematode that parasitises the root systems of tobacco plants, inducing galls and severely reducing yield.

Step 2: Assessment of Other Organisms
*Caenorhabditis elegans* is a free-living model organism, *Wuchereria bancrofti* causes human filariasis, and *Ancylostoma duodenale* is the human hookworm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nematode that infects tobacco roots is *Meloidogyne incognita*.

answer.text: Caenorhabditis elegans
Meloidogyne incognita
Ancylostoma duodenale
Wuchereria bancrofti

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q20 - Natural biological function of RNA interference in eukaryotes

questiontext.text: In all eukaryotic organisms, the cellular mechanism of RNA interference (RNAi) functions naturally as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Natural Role of RNAi
RNA interference (RNAi) is an evolutionary conserved post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanism that occurs in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defense.

Step 2: Target of Defense
It protects eukaryotic cells from foreign RNA invasion, such as infection by RNA viruses or aberrant replication of mobile genetic elements (transposons).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
RNA interference operates in all eukaryotes as a method of cellular defense.

answer.text: An enzymatic cascade that polymerises cellulose microfibrils in cell walls
A transport pathway for importing glucose across the plasma membrane
A method of cellular defense against viral infection and mobile genetic elements
A biosynthetic pathway for assembling ribosomal proteins in the nucleolus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q21 - Molecular mechanism of mRNA silencing by complementary dsRNA

questiontext.text: What is the precise molecular event by which RNA interference (RNAi) prevents the expression of a targeted gene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of RNAi
RNAi involves silencing of a specific messenger RNA (mRNA) by a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) molecule. The dsRNA is processed into small interfering RNAs that guide ribonucleases to bind and cleave the complementary target mRNA.

Step 2: Functional Outcome
Because the targeted mRNA is degraded or blocked, translation cannot occur on ribosomes, resulting in sequence-specific gene silencing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
RNAi silences a gene when a complementary dsRNA molecule binds to a specific mRNA and prevents its translation.

answer.text: Transfer RNA molecules are dephosphorylated, preventing codon recognition
Single-stranded DNA primers bind to nuclear pores and block mRNA export
A complementary dsRNA molecule binds to and silences a specific mRNA, preventing its translation
Endogenous restriction endonucleases cleave the promoter region of the nuclear DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q22 - Agrobacterium mediated sense and antisense RNA expression

questiontext.text: How did researchers engineer host tobacco plants to trigger RNA interference specifically against Meloidogyne incognita?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vector and Construct Design
Scientists used *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* vectors to transfer nematode-specific DNA sequences into the nuclear genome of tobacco plants. The construct was engineered such that transcription produced both sense and anti-sense RNA strands in host plant cells.

Step 2: dsRNA Formation and Silencing
Because these two RNA strands were complementary, they hybridized to form double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). When the nematode fed on the transgenic roots, this dsRNA triggered RNAi within the parasite, silencing its critical mRNA and preventing its survival.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Agrobacterium vectors introduced nematode-specific genes that produced both sense and anti-sense RNA, forming dsRNA that initiated RNAi.

answer.text: Agrobacterium Ti plasmids were used to delete all host nuclear DNA coding for ribosomal RNA
Synthetic single-stranded DNA probes were integrated into host chloroplasts to block photosynthesis in the nematode
Nematode ribosomal RNA was isolated and sprayed onto the leaf foliage to trigger systemic resistance
Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced to produce both sense and anti-sense RNA that formed dsRNA in host cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q23 - Approved recombinant therapeutics in world and in India

questiontext.text: At present, approximately how many recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide, and how many are marketed in India according to NCERT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Statistical Figures in NCERT
NCERT states: 'At present, about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human-use the world over. In India, 12 of these are presently being marketed.'

Step 2: Assessment of Options
The documented numbers are exactly 30 globally and 12 in India.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved worldwide, and 12 are marketed in India.

answer.text: About 15 approved globally, and 6 marketed in India
About 100 approved globally, and 30 marketed in India
About 30 approved globally, and 12 marketed in India
About 50 approved globally, and 25 marketed in India

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q24 - Absence of immunological reactions with recombinant therapeutics

questiontext.text: What is the primary medical benefit of recombinant human therapeutics over similar products isolated from non-human animal sources?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Clinical Benefit of Recombinant Drugs
Therapeutics extracted from animal sources (such as bovine or porcine organs) frequently caused patients to develop allergies or immune reactions against the foreign non-human proteins. Recombinant therapeutics are identical in sequence to human proteins and do not induce unwanted immunological responses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Other Statements
Recombinant proteins do not alter host genes, undergo normal physiological breakdown, and cannot generally be taken orally because gastric and pancreatic proteases degrade them.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The primary benefit is that recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses.

answer.text: They do not induce unwanted immunological responses or foreign-protein allergies
They permanently alter the recipient's nuclear DNA to eliminate future mutations
They can be administered exclusively through oral pills without enzymatic digestion
They are completely resistant to metabolic degradation and circulate permanently in blood

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q25 - Polypeptide structure and linking bonds in mature insulin

questiontext.text: Mature human insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains (chain A and chain B) that are linked together by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structure of Mature Insulin
Mature functional insulin consists of two polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B. These two chains are covalently linked together by disulphide bridges formed between cysteine residues.

Step 2: Evaluation of Other Bonds
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in DNA/RNA, and glycosidic bonds join sugars in carbohydrates.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chains A and B in mature insulin are linked together by disulphide bridges.

answer.text: Hydrogen bonds exclusively
Disulphide bridges
Phosphodiester bonds
Glycosidic linkages

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q26 - Role of C peptide in proinsulin maturation

questiontext.text: What is the key structural difference between mammalian pro-insulin and mature, functional insulin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pro-hormone Maturation Process
In mammals, insulin is synthesized as an inactive pro-hormone (pro-insulin). Pro-insulin contains an extra polypeptide segment known as the C peptide (connecting peptide) connecting chain A and chain B.

Step 2: Post-Translational Processing
During maturation into active insulin, this C peptide is proteolytically cleaved and removed. Mature insulin consists strictly of chains A and B linked by disulphide bonds; it does not contain the C peptide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pro-insulin contains an extra stretch called C peptide that is removed during maturation into insulin.

answer.text: Mature insulin contains the C peptide while pro-insulin lacks it
Pro-insulin contains only chain A, while chain B is added during maturation
Pro-insulin contains an extra stretch called C peptide, which is removed during maturation into insulin
Mature insulin lacks disulphide bonds between chains A and B

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q27 - Eli Lilly milestone in recombinant human insulin synthesis

questiontext.text: In 1983, which company successfully prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and expressed them in E. coli?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Landmark in rDNA Insulin
In 1983, the American pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly prepared two artificial DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of *Escherichia coli*.

Step 2: Production Strategy
Chains A and B were produced separately in bacterial cultures, extracted, and combined by creating disulphide bonds to generate mature human insulin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The American company that accomplished this in 1983 was Eli Lilly.

answer.text: Genentech
Eli Lilly
Biocon
GlaxoSmithKline

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q28 - Bypassing bacterial post translational processing in insulin production

questiontext.text: What major biotechnological hurdle prevented the direct expression of mature human insulin from a complete human pro-insulin cDNA in Escherichia coli, and how was it overcome?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: The Processing Hurdle in Bacteria
Mammalian pro-insulin requires specific endopeptidase enzymes in the Golgi apparatus to cleave out the C peptide and fold chains A and B. Bacteria such as *E. coli* lack this post-translational processing machinery and cannot mature pro-insulin into functional insulin.

Step 2: The Eli Lilly Solution
To solve this, separate synthetic DNA sequences for chain A and chain B were cloned into separate *E. coli* cultures. The expressed chains were isolated independently and then chemically oxidized in vitro to form the correct disulphide bridges.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because bacteria cannot excise the C peptide, chains A and B were expressed separately in E. coli and combined in vitro by creating disulphide bonds.

answer.text: Bacterial ribosomes cannot assemble peptide bonds; this was overcome by using plant Agrobacterium vectors
E. coli lacks the mammalian endopeptidases needed to excise the C peptide; this was overcome by expressing chains A and B separately and joining them in vitro via disulphide bonds
E. coli peptidoglycan hydrolyses insulin polypeptides; this was overcome by expressing pro-insulin in retroviral envelopes
Human pro-insulin genes mutate E. coli plasmids; this was overcome by inserting synthetic bovine insulin sequences

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q29 - Reason insulin cannot be administered orally to patients

questiontext.text: Why must insulin be administered to diabetic patients by injection rather than being taken orally as a tablet?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Protein Nature of Insulin
Insulin is a polypeptide hormone composed of amino acid chains linked by peptide bonds. When ingested orally, it is exposed to gastric hydrochloric acid and digestive endopeptidases and exopeptidases (such as pepsin in the stomach and trypsin/chymotrypsin in the intestine).

Step 2: Digestive Inactivation
These proteolytic enzymes rapidly hydrolyse the peptide bonds, breaking insulin down into free amino acids and destroying its therapeutic endocrine activity before it can reach the bloodstream.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Insulin cannot be administered orally because it is a protein that would be digested by proteolytic enzymes in the alimentary tract.

answer.text: Because its disulphide bridges hydrolyse stomach mucus, leading to acute ulceration
Because oral administration causes spontaneous bacterial transformation in the large intestine
Because it precipitates into toxic insoluble crystals upon contact with salivary amylase
Because being a protein hormone, it would be degraded and digested by proteolytic enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q30 - First clinical gene therapy administered in 1990

questiontext.text: The first clinical gene therapy was administered in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl suffering from which genetic deficiency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Context of First Gene Therapy
The first clinical trial of human gene therapy was performed in 1990 on a 4-year-old girl afflicted with severe combined immunodeficiency caused by adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

Step 2: Significance of the Enzyme
Adenosine deaminase is an essential enzyme for purine metabolism and immune system integrity. Its absence leads to severe immune dysfunction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first clinical gene therapy was administered for adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

answer.text: Sickle cell anaemia
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency
Phenylketonuria (PKU)
Cystic fibrosis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q31 - Need for periodic lymphocyte infusion in gene therapy

questiontext.text: Why does a patient receiving gene therapy for ADA deficiency via genetically engineered lymphocytes require periodic infusions of these cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Protocol of ADA Gene Therapy
In this clinical procedure, peripheral blood lymphocytes from the patient are cultured in vitro, transformed with functional ADA cDNA using a retroviral vector, and infused back into the patient's bloodstream.

Step 2: Reason for Periodic Administration
Because mature, differentiated lymphocytes have a finite natural lifespan (they are not immortal), these engineered cells eventually die. Therefore, the patient must receive periodic infusions of newly transformed lymphocytes to maintain ADA activity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Periodic infusion is necessary because mature lymphocytes are not immortal and have a limited lifespan.

answer.text: Because mature lymphocytes have a limited lifespan and are not immortal
Because the introduced cDNA is eliminated during each mitotic cell division
Because the retroviral vector continuously mutates the ADA cDNA into inactive fragments
Because circulating plasma proteases digest the nucleus of engineered lymphocytes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q32 - Requirements for a permanent cure for ADA deficiency

questiontext.text: While enzyme replacement therapy and bone marrow transplantation can treat ADA deficiency, under what condition can gene therapy provide a permanent cure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Limitations of Current Treatments
Enzyme replacement therapy (periodic injections of functional ADA) and bone marrow transplantation can treat ADA deficiency, but neither provides a completely curative outcome in all patients.

Step 2: Basis of a Permanent Cure
A permanent cure can be achieved if the functional ADA gene isolated from bone marrow cells is introduced into target stem cells during early embryonic development. In an early embryo, the inserted gene will be inherited and expressed in all subsequent cellular lineages forming the immune system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A permanent cure is possible if the ADA gene from marrow cells is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages.

answer.text: If functional ADA enzyme is administered orally three times daily from early childhood
If all bone marrow stem cells in the adult patient are irradiated and replaced with E. coli cultures
If the functional ADA gene isolated from marrow cells is introduced into host cells at early embryonic stages
If retroviral vectors are injected directly into the adult thymus gland after puberty

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q33 - Vector used in introducing functional ADA cDNA

questiontext.text: Which biological vector was utilized to introduce functional ADA cDNA into the cultured lymphocytes of the patient during clinical gene therapy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vector for Human Gene Delivery
In the 1990 clinical gene therapy trial, researchers used a disarmed retroviral vector to efficiently integrate and express the functional human ADA cDNA within the patient's cultured lymphocytes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Other Vectors
*Agrobacterium* vectors are used in plants, and *Bacillus thuringiensis* plasmids are not therapeutic gene delivery vectors in humans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A retroviral vector was used to deliver functional ADA cDNA into the patient's lymphocytes.

answer.text: Bacteriophage M13
Bacillus thuringiensis crystal plasmid
A retroviral vector
Agrobacterium Ti plasmid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q34 - Comparison of PCR, ELISA, and probe-based molecular diagnosis

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately evaluates the distinct biochemical principles underlying PCR, ELISA, and probe-based autoradiography in molecular diagnosis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Operational Principles in Molecular Diagnosis
PCR operates by enzymatically amplifying minute amounts of target pathogen DNA or RNA, allowing diagnosis before clinical symptoms emerge. ELISA operates on the principle of antigen-antibody interactions, detecting pathogen antigens or host-synthesized antibodies. Single-stranded radioactive probes in autoradiography hybridize to complementary normal sequences, failing to bind to mutated sequences due to mismatch.

Step 2: Comparative Evaluation
Distinguishing nucleic acid amplification (PCR), serological binding (ELISA), and hybridisation failure (probe autoradiography) correctly unifies the molecular diagnostic tools covered in NCERT.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
PCR amplifies trace nucleic acids, ELISA detects antigen-antibody interactions, and autoradiography detects mutated genes via loss of probe complementarity.

answer.text: PCR, ELISA, and autoradiography all rely exclusively on the lytic activity of Bacillus thuringiensis crystal proteins
PCR hydrolyses foreign protein capsids, ELISA measures DNA optical density, and autoradiography repairs point mutations
PCR amplifies trace nucleic acids exponentially, ELISA detects antigen-antibody interactions, and autoradiography detects mutated genes via loss of probe complementarity
ELISA amplifies viral genomes, PCR detects antibody-antigen complexes, and autoradiography purifies pro-insulin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q35 - Biochemical principle of ELISA diagnostic test

questiontext.text: The widely used molecular diagnostic technique ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay) is fundamentally based on which principle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Underlying Principle of ELISA
ELISA is based on the specificity of antigen-antibody interactions. A pathogen infection is detected either by identifying the presence of specific antigens (proteins or glycoproteins) of the pathogen or by detecting antibodies produced by the host immune system in response to the pathogen.

Step 2: Evaluation of Distractors
Probe hybridization is the principle of autoradiography and blotting, not ELISA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ELISA is fundamentally based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction.

answer.text: Centrifugal sedimentation velocity of viral genomes
Antigen-antibody interaction
Proteolytic cleavage of polypeptide disulphide bridges
Complementary base pairing of radioactive probes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q36 - Failure of mutated clones to appear in autoradiography

questiontext.text: In a molecular diagnostic procedure, a radioactive single-stranded DNA probe is hybridized to cellular DNA clones followed by detection using autoradiography. Why does a clone carrying a mutated gene fail to appear on the photographic film?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Probe Hybridisation
A radioactive single-stranded probe is designed with a specific sequence complementary to the normal, wild-type gene sequence.

Step 2: Effect of Mutation on Hybridisation
When a mutation is present in a clone's target gene, the loss of sequence complementarity prevents the radioactive probe from annealing to that DNA. Because no radioactive probe binds, no radioactivity exposes the photographic film, and the clone does not appear on the autoradiograph.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mutated clone does not appear because the radioactive probe lacks complementarity with the mutated gene and fails to hybridise.

answer.text: Mutated DNA fragments are chemically degraded by the photographic emulsion developer
The radioactive probe lacks base-pairing complementarity with the mutated gene and fails to hybridise with it
The mutated gene absorbs the emitted radiation, preventing photographic film exposure
The mutation converts the radioactive isotope of the probe into non-radioactive carbon

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q37 - Dominant species among existing transgenic animals

questiontext.text: Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals produced for biomedical research belong to which animal group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Statistical Dominance of Transgenic Mice
Although transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, and fish have been successfully produced, over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

Step 2: Scientific Reasons
Mice are preferred due to their small size, short generation interval, high fecundity, and well-characterized genetics.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

answer.text: Rabbits
Mice
Rats
Pigs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q38 - Transgenic animals in studying physiology and development

questiontext.text: How are transgenic animals specifically designed to study normal body physiology and development?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological Investigation Using Transgenics
Transgenic animals are engineered to investigate gene regulation and physiological development. For example, introducing genes from other species that modify the expression of complex growth factors like insulin-like growth factor allows researchers to observe the downstream anatomical and physiological consequences, identifying the factor's biological role.

Step 2: Critique of Other Options
Researchers do not eliminate all hormones, halt embryonic cell division, or delete mitochondrial genomes for this purpose.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are used to study physiology by introducing genes that alter the formation of factors like insulin-like growth factor and studying the resulting effects.

answer.text: By removing all endogenous hormones and replacing them exclusively with microbial toxins
By eliminating cell division in embryonic tissues to observe adult organ arrest
By introducing foreign genes that alter the formation of specific growth factors (e.g., insulin-like growth factor) and observing resulting biological effects
By deleting mitochondrial DNA to determine if oxidative respiration is essential

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q39 - Human disease models established using transgenic animals

questiontext.text: Transgenic animal models have been specially created to study the pathophysiology and investigate novel treatments for which set of human diseases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: NCERT Enumeration of Disease Models
NCERT specifically highlights that transgenic animal models exist today for many complex human diseases, including cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's disease.

Step 2: Assessment of Alternatives
Nutritional deficiencies (scurvy, rickets) or infectious bacterial/protozoan diseases (amoebiasis, typhoid) are not the primary focus of these complex genetic disease models.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Transgenic models exist for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's disease.

answer.text: Amoebiasis, cholera, typhoid, and malaria
Polio, smallpox, ringworm, and common cold
Xerophthalmia, scurvy, rickets, and beri-beri
Cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's disease

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q40 - Production of alpha 1 antitrypsin to treat emphysema

questiontext.text: Transgenic animals have been engineered to produce the human protein alpha-1-antitrypsin, which is therapeutically used to treat:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Production of Therapeutic Biological Products
Transgenic animals can act as bioreactors to synthesize valuable human proteins. The human protein alpha-1-antitrypsin has been successfully produced in transgenic animals and is used clinically to treat emphysema.

Step 2: Related Attempts
Similar attempts are being made to produce therapeutics for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Alpha-1-antitrypsin is used for the treatment of emphysema.

answer.text: Rheumatoid arthritis
Cystic fibrosis
Emphysema
Phenylketonuria

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q41 - Transgenic cow Rosie producing human protein enriched milk

questiontext.text: In 1997, the first transgenic cow, Rosie, was produced. What was the distinctive characteristic and nutritional significance of her milk?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Rosie the Transgenic Cow
In 1997, Rosie was developed as the first transgenic cow. Her milk was enriched with a human protein, containing 2.4 grams of human protein per litre.

Step 2: Nutritional Value
The milk contained the human protein alpha-lactalbumin. This rendered the milk nutritionally much more balanced and suitable for human infants than natural cow milk, which has a different protein profile.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Rosie produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre) containing human alpha-lactalbumin, which was nutritionally more balanced for human babies.

answer.text: She produced milk containing human alpha-1-antitrypsin to cure emphysema in newborn calves
She produced milk free of all lipids and proteins, consisting solely of sterile glucose solution
She produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre) containing human alpha-lactalbumin, making it nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk
She produced milk containing 24 grams per litre of human insulin, which could be ingested orally by diabetic infants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q42 - Transgenic mice in vaccine safety and toxicity testing

questiontext.text: Transgenic animals are utilized in vaccine safety testing and chemical toxicity testing. Which statement correctly evaluates their application in these domains according to NCERT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vaccine Safety Testing
Transgenic mice are developed and tested for the safety of vaccines, such as the polio vaccine, before clinical use in humans. If validated, they could replace the traditional use of monkeys.

Step 2: Chemical Safety (Toxicity) Testing
In toxicity testing, transgenic animals are engineered to carry foreign genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances than wild-type animals. Exposure to chemicals produces clear toxicity symptoms in significantly less time.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Transgenic mice test polio vaccine safety before human use, and animals carrying sensitive genes yield toxicity testing results in less time.

answer.text: Transgenic monkeys have completely replaced transgenic mice because primates do not express human receptors
Transgenic pigs are used to test the safety of all viral vaccines because they do not possess an active immune system
Chemical toxicity testing requires transgenic animals that are completely immune and insensitive to all toxic compounds
Transgenic mice are used to test the safety of the polio vaccine before human trials, and animals carrying sensitive genes provide toxicity results in less time

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q43 - Statutory role and functions of GEAC in India

questiontext.text: In India, which governmental organisation makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Statutory Role of GEAC
The Indian Government established the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC).

Step 2: Mandate
The GEAC is mandated to make authoritative decisions regarding the validity and ethical compliance of genetic modification research, and the biosafety of releasing genetically modified organisms and their products into the environment for public services.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The organisation is the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC).

answer.text: Genomic Environmental Advisory Council (GEAC)
Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC)
Global Ecological Assessment Commission (GEAC)
Governmental Ethics and Agriculture Committee (GEAC)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q44 - Definition of biopiracy involving indigenous bioresources

questiontext.text: The unauthorized use of bio-resources and traditional knowledge by multinational companies without proper authorization and without compensatory payment is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Biopiracy
Biopiracy is defined as the commercial exploitation or patenting of biological resources and associated indigenous traditional knowledge by multinational corporations or organisations without obtaining prior informed consent and without providing equitable compensatory payment to the source nations and indigenous communities.

Step 2: Distinction from Other Terms
Bioremediation is environmental cleanup using microbes, and biofortification is breeding crops for higher nutritional quality.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The unauthorized exploitation of bio-resources without compensation is termed biopiracy.

answer.text: Biofortification
Bioremediation
Biopiracy
Bioprospecting

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q45 - Rich diversity of Indian rice and Basmati varieties

questiontext.text: According to NCERT, what is the estimated richness of rice varieties in India, and how many documented varieties of aromatic Basmati rice are grown in the country?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Rice Diversity Statistics in NCERT
NCERT states: 'There are an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone. The diversity of rice in India is one of the richest in the world. Basmati rice is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour and 27 documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India.'

Step 2: Assessment of Options
The accurate recorded figures are 200,000 rice varieties and 27 documented varieties of Basmati.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
India has an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice and 27 documented varieties of Basmati.

answer.text: An estimated 50,000 varieties of rice, with 14 documented varieties of Basmati
An estimated 1,000,000 varieties of rice, with 108 documented varieties of Basmati
An estimated 200,000 varieties of rice, with 27 documented varieties of Basmati
An estimated 20,000 varieties of rice, with 5 documented varieties of Basmati

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q46 - 1997 US patent controversy regarding Indian Basmati rice

questiontext.text: In 1997, an American company obtained patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. On what factual basis was this patent claimed as a novel invention?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: The 1997 Basmati Patent Case
In 1997, a US company was granted patent rights on Basmati rice lines by the US Patent and Trademark Office. The company had crossed traditional Indian Basmati varieties with semi-dwarf lines and claimed the resulting hybrid as their own proprietary invention.

Step 2: The Biopiracy Dispute
This patent extended to functional equivalents, threatening to restrict Indian farmers and exporters from selling authentic Basmati abroad, despite Basmati having been documented in ancient Indian folklore, texts, and poetry for centuries.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The patent was claimed because the company crossed traditional Indian Basmati with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed the result as an invention.

answer.text: The company proved that Basmati rice had never been cultivated or documented anywhere in Asia
The company isolated the wild ancestor of Basmati from deep oceanic hydrothermal vents
The company crossed traditional Indian Basmati rice with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed it as an invention or novelty
The company inserted synthetic Bt cryIAc genes into Basmati to render it pest resistant

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q47 - Traditional Indian herbal medicines targeted for unauthorized patents

questiontext.text: Apart from Basmati rice, which traditional Indian herbal products have faced attempts by foreign organisations to patent their longstanding medicinal and commercial uses?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Patent Attempts on Indian Traditional Knowledge
NCERT notes: 'Several attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, e.g., turmeric neem.'

Step 2: Relevance to Traditional Knowledge
Turmeric has been traditionally used in India for wound healing, and neem has been used as a natural biopesticide and antiseptic. Foreign patents on these traditional applications represent classic examples of biopiracy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Turmeric and neem are the traditional herbal medicines targeted for unauthorized patents.

answer.text: Coffee and tea
Wheat and barley
Sunflower and mustard
Turmeric and neem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q48 - Legislative measures under Indian Patents Bill second amendment

questiontext.text: To counter biopiracy and protect indigenous bio-resources and traditional knowledge, what legislative step was enacted by the Indian Parliament as highlighted in NCERT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Legislative Defense Against Biopiracy
To safeguard national sovereign rights over biological resources and traditional knowledge, the Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill.

Step 2: Key Provisions
This amendment considers critical issues including patent terms, emergency provisions, and incentives for domestic research and development initiatives, ensuring fair benefit-sharing and preventing unauthorized foreign patenting.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, covering patent terms, emergency provisions, and research and development initiatives.

answer.text: Prohibiting the cultivation of all varieties of rice and wheat in national agricultural fields
Clearing the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, incorporating patent terms, emergency provisions, and research and development initiatives
Dissolving the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee and eliminating environmental safety standards
Banning all clinical research on recombinant DNA vaccines and therapeutics within India
